title: Wikimedia Commons New Mexico New Mexico law puts donor privacy in Supreme Court spotlight
body: A new piece in The Federalist is putting national attention on a New Mexico campaign finance law that critics say forces civic groups to choose between speaking about elected officials and exposing private donors to the government. The article, written by Marc Wheat and Mitchell Bahnsen, focuses on Rio Grande Foundation v. Oliver, a First Amendment case now being pushed toward U.S. Supreme Court review after the Tenth Circuit upheld New Mexico’s donor-disclosure rules. At issue is a planned Rio Grande Foundation legislative scorecard — the type of voting record civic groups, newspapers, watchdogs, and taxpayer organizations have published for decades. The scorecard would have informed New Mexicans about how lawmakers voted on key issues. It did not tell voters which candidate to support or oppose. But because the scorecard named candidates and was planned within a pre-election window, New Mexico’s Campaign Reporting Act treated the communication as an “independent expenditure,” triggering donor-disclosure requirements. As The Federalist put it, “A voting scorecard shouldn’t trigger a government demand for supporters’ home addresses.” Under the law, an organization that spends more than $1,000 on certain communications referencing a candidate or ballot measure near an election can be forced to disclose donors who gave more than $5,000 during a two-year election cycle, unless those donors affirmatively opt out. Critics say that structure turns ordinary issue speech into a trap. A donor may support a nonprofit’s broad work on taxes, government transparency, education, or free markets without realizing that a future mailing could place his or her name and address in a government disclosure system. “A $5,000 donation to a nonprofit organization that publishes voting records is hardly identical to a campaign contribution or an endorsement of any candidate, yet the state treats them the same,” Wheat and Bahnsen wrote. That is the heart of the controversy. Supporters of disclosure laws argue voters have a right to know who is funding political messages. But opponents say New Mexico’s law goes far beyond campaign advocacy by sweeping in issue groups that merely mention public officials close to an election. The Rio Grande Foundation says the law chilled its speech. In Supreme Court filings, the group said it planned to mail its “Freedom Index,” a legislative scorecard tracking lawmakers’ votes, to thousands of voters within 60 days of the 2020 general election. It did not do so because of the state’s donor-disclosure requirements. The group argues that donor privacy is part of the First Amendment right to free association. The concern is not abstract. Donors to controversial causes can face harassment, threats, employment pressure, social retaliation, and efforts to punish them for supporting disfavored speech. The Federalist piece pointed to the landmark 1958 case NAACP v. Alabama, in which the Supreme Court stopped Alabama from forcing the NAACP to disclose its membership lists. The Court recognized that forced disclosure could expose members to retaliation and chill association. The article also cited Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta, the 2021 Supreme Court case striking down California’s donor-disclosure regime for charities. In that case, the Court held that California’s requirement burdened First Amendment rights and was not narrowly tailored. For conservatives, the New Mexico case raises the same basic question: why should citizens have to surrender privacy to support a nonprofit that publishes a voting record? The Federalist also invoked McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission, in which the Supreme Court wrote that “anonymity is a shield from the tyranny of the majority.” That line is especially relevant in a political climate where people are routinely targeted for donations, statements, affiliations, and even past political positions. The Federalist noted that donors to California’s Proposition 8 faced harassment after their names became public, and that Mozilla co-founder Brendan Eich was later forced out of his own company after his donation to the measure resurfaced. The Tenth Circuit sided with New Mexico, finding the disclosure requirements sufficiently tied to the state’s interest in informing voters about who funds large election-related communications near elections. But the Rio Grande Foundation and its supporters argue that the lower courts are applying too weak a standard to laws that burden anonymous speech and association. They are asking the Supreme Court to clarify whether laws forcing disclosure of political association should face strict scrutiny, the highest level of constitutional review, rather than the more flexible “exacting scrutiny” standard that courts have often applied. The case now puts New Mexico at the center of a national free speech fight. For Piñon Post readers, the stakes are obvious. If a nonprofit can be forced to expose donors simply because it mails a voting scorecard too close to an election, that gives government enormous power to chill criticism of politicians at the exact moment voters are paying attention. New Mexico voters have every right to know how their elected officials voted. And citizens have every right to support groups that publish that information without being placed on a government list. title: Tequila Rain savors return to Vegas
body: The variety band Tequila Rain takes the stage during the Fiestas de Las Vegas on Sunday at Plaza Park.  The variety band Tequila Rain takes the stage during the Fiestas de Las Vegas on Sunday at Plaza Park. Tequila Rain is making up for lost time. After not performing in Las Vegas for years, members of the award-winning, Northern New Mexico-based band can now say they have played at Fiestas de Las Vegas for two consecutive years. Tequila Rain also performed during the city’s Father’s Day concert June 21 at Plaza Park. During the 2026 Fiestas de Las Vegas, Tequila Rain played a range of styles at Plaza Park, including classic rock, cumbias and Tex-Mex. They wrapped up their set on Sunday with “Sweet Caroline,” a song made famous by Neil Diamond. Tequila Rain mostly plays cover songs; however, guitarist and founding member Joe Valencia has contributed his own compositions to the band’s repertoire. One such song is “Venenosa Mujer,” which Valencia described as a Tejano song. Another of Valencia’s compositions is “Palabras Bonitas,” which, he said, has “done really well for us.” He said the slow-paced, romantic ballad is often requested at weddings. Valencia described Tequila Rain as a variety band. He said Tequila Rain covers a wide range of genres in an attempt to appeal to the most people. “We try to cover as much ground as we can,” Valencia said. “New Mexico is a melting pot of people that like different music. We try to please as many people as we can.” The band’s name reflects this attempt to appeal to a diverse audience.  Valencia said country music was popular in 1993, the year the group was formed. A name like Tequila Rain fit in with the country music genre and helped the band get into bars where that music was played. The group’s different iterations over the years – caused by a turnaround of its musicians – has also aided their ability to delve into different styles and genres of music. Joe Valencia and his brother, vocalist and bass player Brian Valencia, are the only two members of the group that have remained constant over the years. Originally from Pecos, Joe and Brian Valencia started Tequila Rain after breaking away from their previous band, Bandolero. Since then, they have seen a large number of musicians come and go. “It’s tough to keep musicians,” Joe Valencia said. “Especially if they’re good,” Brian Valencia chimed in. He said that the band has benefited from the different sounds that different musicians have given it. “You learn something new from every musician you get,” Joe Valencia said. “Hopefully, when they leave, they take something that they’ve learned from you also.” Tequila Rain currently includes keyboardist and saxophone player Steve (Mertyle) Merhege from Española and drummer Paul Fernandes from Medanales. The Valencia brothers have recorded three albums with Tequila Rain and six albums with their previous band, Bandolero. While a quick Internet search states that the band has been honored and nominated for a number of awards, Joe Valencia remained humble about them, stating that the band does not “advertise awards.” He said this is because, while getting awards is nice, “they gather dust.” “We want people to hear our music,” Joe Valencia said. “That’s the bottom line.” Brian Valencia noted the hard work and dedication it takes to perform – such as rehearsing and memorizing the songs. But, he said, all the smiling faces at the Fiestas “is what makes it all worth it.” Your comment has been submitted.  Reported There was a problem reporting this. title: ‘Unique Crosses and Creations’ offers beautiful wares to Fiestas attendees
body: Cindy Fernandez shows off metal ant toys that she sells through her business, Unique Crosses and Creations. Fernandez set up a booth during this year’s Fiestas de Las Vegas over the weekend.  Cindy Fernandez shows off metal ant toys that she sells through her business, Unique Crosses and Creations. Fernandez set up a booth during this year’s Fiestas de Las Vegas over the weekend. A variety of shiny, colorful insect figurines – ladybugs, spiders and ants – lined one side of the display for Unique Crosses and Creations, a traveling business that offered wares during the recent Fiestas de Las Vegas. The other side of the booth was lined with a variety of crosses embellished with stones and paint. Cindy Fernandez, owner and operator of Unique Crosses and Creations, said the crosses are the only artifacts she typically works on. Other objects for sale, including necklaces, pendants, household decorations and rosaries, just to name a few of the items at her booth, are not made by Fernandez.  However, everything she sells is still very much part of the business that started as a hobby “for the weekends.” It is now something she does to keep herself, and others, happy. Fernandez said that, following a motor vehicle accident about 15 years ago, she needed something to devote energy to. “I needed a hobby,” she said. “I needed something to do.” She said she was inspired by her daughter, Shawna Fernandez-Wilkins, a self-taught artist who makes her own jewelry and attends crafts shows with her creations. Fernandez then had the idea of Unique Crosses and Creations, a business that operated out of her own garage in Springer. It’s never been a brick-and-mortar establishment; Fernandez chooses to bring her colorful wares to different events throughout the United States. This was her third year attending the Fiestas de Las Vegas, Fernandez said. She said that of all the events she attends, the Fiestas are her “favorite show to do, for sure.” “I just love listening to the music and meeting kind people,” Fernandez said of the Fiestas. title: Screenshot, CNN New Mexico Dems abandon scandal-plagued Platner after Heinrich stood by him
body: New Mexico’s Democrat senators are facing new scrutiny over their handling of Maine Democrat Senate nominee Graham Platner after a rape allegation sent national Democrats fleeing from a candidate many in the party had recently tried to rally behind. Platner, the Democrat nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine, is accused by a woman he previously dated of drunkenly forcing her to have sex after she told him to stop, according to reporting cited by the Associated Press. Platner denies the allegation. The latest report triggered a political crisis for Democrats in a must-win Senate race against Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins. Senate Democrat leaders, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, prominent progressives, and Maine Democrat officials quickly began calling for Platner to leave the race. But the collapse comes after some Democrats, including U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who “proudly” endorsed the scandal-plagued candidate, had already defended Platner through earlier scandals involving a Nazi-linked tattoo, inflammatory online posts, sexually explicit messages, and allegations involving past relationships. During a CNN appearance with Wolf Blitzer before the latest rape allegation surfaced, Heinrich defended Platner as a man who had grown from his past. “Graham has made a lot of mistakes in his life,” Heinrich said. “He’s owned those mistakes… that’s what leadership looks like.” MARTIN HEINRICH: “Graham [Platner] has made a lot of mistakes in his life…He's owned those mistakes…that's what leadership looks like.” pic.twitter.com/WAYIKNRGow That quote now looks very different after the newest allegation sent Democrats scrambling to distance themselves from Platner. According to the AP, the woman, Jenny Racicot, accused Platner of entering her home in 2021 while drunk and assaulting her. Racicot said she had been in an on-and-off relationship with Platner but cut off contact after that night and later told him the encounter was not consensual. “He violated multiple layers of consent that night,” Racicot said in a CNN interview, according to the AP. Platner denied the allegation in a video statement. “Any accusation of non-consensual behavior is categorically false,” Platner said. He also said he was considering the future of his campaign. “Regardless of the inaccuracy of the reporting but mindful of the political reality it will inflict, we’re taking the time to reflect on the best path forward,” Platner said. For Democrats, the political reality was immediate. U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand issued a joint statement calling on Platner to withdraw. “Graham Platner needs to immediately withdraw as the Democratic nominee for Senate and allow Maine Democrats the opportunity to choose a new candidate who can defeat Susan Collins,” they said. The DSCC also said it would not spend money on the Maine Senate race if Platner remained the nominee. Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said Maine Democrats should choose a new nominee. Rep. Ro Khanna, who had previously supported Platner, withdrew his endorsement. “I’ve been very clear that sexual assault or violence against women is a red line,” Khanna said. “These allegations are very serious and credible. Graham Platner should drop out from the race. I am withdrawing my endorsement.” U.S. Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Ruben Gallego of Arizona also pulled their support and called for Platner to exit the race. Maine Democratic Party leaders joined the calls for him to withdraw. The pressure is especially intense because Maine law allows Platner to be replaced on the ballot only if he withdraws by July 13, with a replacement nominee named by July 27. The latest allegation is not the first controversy surrounding Platner. Before winning the Democrat nomination, Platner had already faced scrutiny for a chest tattoo recognized as a Nazi symbol, which he later covered up. He also reportedly faced criticism over explicit messages sent to women shortly after getting married and a history of inflammatory online comments. In one 2013 Reddit post, Platner wrote that people should not get so drunk “they wind up having sex with someone they don’t mean to” and suggested sexual assault victims should “just take some responsibility for themselves.” He has since apologized for the post and said he no longer believes those things. The New York Times also reported on volatile relationships with former girlfriends, including one allegation that an argument became physical. Platner denied that allegation. New Mexico’s other Democrat senator, Ben Ray Luján, also addressed Platner before the latest wave of calls for withdrawal. Luján said Platner needed to be “forthright” and “honest” with voters. “Look, he’s the nominee right now,” Luján said. “He has to go and earn the trust of voters. And just like every other candidate has to do as well.” That careful language stopped short of fully cutting Platner loose at the time. But after the latest allegation, the Democrat Party’s calculus changed almost overnight. Now, Lujan wrote via X, “The American people deserve leaders they can trust. These allegations are serious, demand accountability, and make that trust impossible. Graham Platner should withdraw from the Senate race.” The American people deserve leaders they can trust. These allegations are serious, demand accountability, and make that trust impossible. Graham Platner should withdraw from the Senate race. For New Mexicans, the episode raises an obvious question: why were national Democrats, including Heinrich, so willing to treat Platner’s long list of earlier controversies as forgivable “mistakes” until the political pressure became impossible to ignore? Heinrich’s “that’s what leadership looks like” defense is now being viewed in a harsher light as Democrats rush to push Platner off the ballot. Luján’s insistence that Platner needed to earn trust also reflects the awkward position Senate Democrats found themselves in: trying to hold a crucial seat while managing a nominee with extensive baggage. Platner remains the Democrat nominee unless he withdraws. Collins, the Republican incumbent, responded briefly to the allegation. “These allegations are appalling,” Collins said. “Nevertheless, it is not up to me to choose the Democratic nominee for Senate.” For Democrats, that choice may now define one of the most important Senate races in the country. And for New Mexico’s senators, the question is no longer just whether Platner can survive. It is why Democrats ever tried to explain away so many warning signs in the first place. title: Hull Stuck In Neutral After First Month Of Guv Campaign; Haaland Money Machine Whirs Away As GOP Hopes For Unforced Errors, Plus: Checking Power; LFC Seen As Key Player For Moderates As GOP Fades And Progressives Rise
body: Hull & HaalandThere will be no early start for Gregg Hull. The '26 GOP gubernatorial nominee is stuck in neutral following the first month of the campaign, lacking the financial muscle to engage Democrat Deb Haaland whose well-oiled money machine has already churned out over $13 million with more to come. The latest campaign finance reports covering May 27 to June 27 show Hull did not get much of a bump from his June 2 primary victory over two primary opponents. He reports raising $349,000 for the month and cash on hand of $298,000 heading into the final four months before the Nov. 3 election. While Haaland hauls in millions, Hull has yet to hit the $1 million milestone with a total of $945,000 raised. In his post-primary report his lack of big money from big oil continued to stand out. That traditional funding source that backed away from Hull in the primary may have dried up even more after the head of the NM Oil and Gas Association warned that the race appears out of reach for the Republican. Hull's low fuel tank means no early TV or other high-profile messaging in the weeks ahead as he faces the arduous task of increasing Haaland's negatives. Meanwhile, if she chooses, Haaland could go up on the air later this month and stay there for the duration.  Haaland reports raising another $1.1 million in the latest period with donations again coming from across the nation as she attempts to become the first Native American governor in state history and the first Native American woman governor in US history. She is spending the money almost as fast as she raises it, reporting a relatively modest cash on hand of $2.278 million from the over $13 million total raised. Still, that is nearly an 8 to 1 cash advantage over Hull and no problem raising more as Hull struggles to convince donors that he has a shot at victory. He does have a shot but at a very narrow target and the gun is not in his hands. Haaland will need unforced errors if the race is to become a race. Fortunately for the former Rio Rancho mayor, she has shown that she is capable of the major misstep. Her meandering testimony before congressional committees while serving as Secretary of Interior being one example. But Hull forcing her to slip will be like trying to open a tin can with his fingernails. Already her handlers are putting her in a protective cocoon by issuing statements in response to media inquires rather than conducting interviews.LIGHT GUV ACTIONA surprise that caused the Haaland-Hull contest to get a second look would be unlikely but not unheard of. We just had a mild one when Maggie Toulouse Oliver, the winner of the Democratic nomination for lieutenant governor, said she would abandon her candidacy because of health reasons. The Democratic party's State Central Committee will meet July 25 to fill the vacancy. Haaland has tried to make their choice a fait accompli by endorsing Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard for the job. But the persistence of ABQ Dem state Senator Harold Pope in seeking the post after finishing second to Toulouse Oliver at the June primary is causing concern in the Haaland camp.  That Pope would be the first Black to be on a major party gubernatorial ticket makes the situation more sticky.Garcia Richard--with Haaland's help--is expected to defeat Pope but if she did not the Haaland glass jaw would be exposed and perhaps cause prospective Hull donors to get off their depression meds and onto the campaign trail. POLLING  There has been no early polling in the race but Polymarket bettors who nailed the outcome of the primary election now give Haaland an 86 percent chance of winning. The Cook Political Report in DC rates the race "likely Democrat" just below "solid Dem" which would signify a nearly sure thing. Republicans can usually count on 42-46 percent of the vote in a statewide election. The fear they have is that Haaland's money and presumed polling advantage could push her winning total past 60 percent, a feat last seen in 2006 when Gov. Richardson was re-elected with 69 percent support. The saving grace is that Hull comes from the vote-laden ABQ metro area, is reasonably articulate and won the primary with demonstrated appeal in rural areas as well as the cities. He should, with some money and messaging, tamp down the Haaland landslide narrative by Labor Day and then start that long hard, climb to break out of the usual GOP range.CHECKING POWERLFC Director SalleeShould Haaland win she would be expected to expand the hold of progressives on state government as Republicans continue to struggle to be a factor. However conservatives and moderates could still have a powerful voice at the Roundhouse.The authoritative Legislative Finance Committee (LFC) has been issuing some interesting reports that question the effectiveness of increased state spending in matters such as behavioral health. Under the leadership of LFC Director Charles Sallee the emphasis on accountability has become more pronounced and stands in contrast to an increasingly progressive legislature. The LFC was founded in the 50's as a counterweight to executive power and has been a major player since. By it's nature it has leaned conservative and has taken heat for it in recent years as the state  languished. Today the problem is not a lack of funds to stimulate the economy or pursue new programs, it is the immense amount of money flooding into Santa Fe that is overwhelming policy makers. The news that the state's sovereign fund is about to total a staggering $75 billion will surely reframe the discussion over the state's financial future--or should. There is obviously more room for risk-taking to resolve the social conditions crisis that haunts the state. That means the LFC must not be ideologically focused but instead insist on fulsome accountability as it did with the behavioral health study.  Haaland would like to advance universal health care and affordable housing. Hull would like major tax reform. Both are sweeping and expensive platforms that have their merits and will be encouraged. But there is increasing apprehension that the once-in-history oil windfall could come and go with the state remaining a backwater economically and socially. That's where the LFC comes into play. Validating what works and what doesn't and doing it with urgency is the accountability that can keep the ball rolling in search of lasting solutions. They seem to be up for the challenge. This is the Home of New Mexico PoliticsE-mail your news and comments. (newsguy@yahoo.com) Interested in reaching New Mexico's most informed audience? title: Old News June 27-July 3: Stories from the past 147 years
body: Front page of the July 3, 1975 issue of the Las Vegas Optic.  Front page of the July 3, 1975 issue of the Las Vegas Optic. The agreement of the organization known as the Rociada Mining District was left for filing at the recorder’s office today, and it will be recorded in Mora county, also. There are twenty-seven signers to the agreement, which has for its purpose the regulation of the mines in that district and the petitioning of the legislature for the appointment of a mine inspector; for the sale of dated powder (providing a fine for selling powder that is not dated); for recognition of the mining district; giving privilege of election by citizens of a local recorder, to record all local claims in the said district, and for the regulation of the water rights. The agreement provides also for a miners’ meeting once each year. The signers, or members of the district, include some of the most prominent men in the neighborhood, besides Chicago investors.  With the new name given the rodeo but the same old spirit of Reunion crowds, folk from the range country and nearby towns began to flock into Las Vegas last night and this morning for the 18th showing of Las Vegas’ entertainment during three days of the Fourth of July week-end. There seemed to be no lessening in the number of people lining the streets this morning as the cowboys’ parade moved through New Town and to the Plaza. Plenty of noisy riders accompanied by a few floats inaugurated the annual celebration which began shortly after two-thirty o’clock with the rodeo at Cowboy Park. Threatening weather, frequent damper of Fourth of July attendance, seems to have discouraged but few of the visitors and a good crowd is expected for the opening day with larger numbers here for Sunday and the Fourth. The programs have been well arranged and with 33 contestants of reputation entered, the rodeo contests should provide plenty of action and thrills for the crowds. This has been a lean year among the rodeo contest promoters of the west and a lot of “top hands” came to Las Vegas for the show hoping to make up for lack of opportunities elsewhere.  The first state-supported psychiatric clinic will begin operations within the next two weeks at the new diagnostic and treatment center at the State Hospital, according to an announcement made today by Dr. C.G. Stillinger, superintendent. Initially the clinic will concentrate on the northeastern area of the state, although applications will not be turned down from other parts of the state, he said. The clinic building, located on the State Hospital grounds, was built two years ago, one-third of the construction costs provided by federal Hill-Burton funds. Due to a shortage of professional staff at the Hospital it has been impossible to get the clinic into operation. Dr. Stillinger stated that the services of a psychiatrist have now been secured on a part-time basis. Dr. William F. Sears, a newly arrived psychiatrist in private practice at Los Alamos, will conduct the clinic, with the assistance of members of the Hospital’s psychological and social services staff. “We are going to have to feel our way in this new project and until we know the kinds of problems and the volume of cases we will be dealing with, the clinic will have to operate on a limited basis,” Dr. Stillinger pointed out. title: Pre-registration open for Missoula Children’s Theatre production in Las Vegas
body: It’s time for the parents and grandparents to sign up their school-aged family members to participate in this year’s edition of the Missoula Children’s Theatre’s summer workshop and performance in Las Vegas, according to Aneata O’Brien, who is coordinating the event for the third year.  Participation in this production is free. Preparation for this year’s show, The Little Mermaid, begins, July 27, in Ilfeld Auditorium on the Highlands University Campus.  The students will audition Monday morning and rehearse portions of every day, leading up to a performance at Ilfeld at 6 p.m, Friday, July 31. O’Brien said parents and grandparents or guardians can pre-register student performers in advance at lasvegasartsouncil.org@gmail.com.  Enrollment is limited to 60 aspiring young actors. Preregistration is open now.  Auditions for all partipants will be from 9:45 to noon on Monday, July 27 at Ilfeld.  “These auditions are stress-free and everyone who auditions will get a part in the production,” said O’Brien.  No preparation is needed. Participation is open to all students who will be in Grades 1 through 12 this fall. Among the roles to be cast are the Little Mermaid, Celia, her three sisters, Delia, Amelia, and Ophelia, Gil, the Merboy next door; the royal family including the Prince, the King and the Queen; the poetic Town Criers, dynamic Sea Scouts, snoopy Seasiders, the country singin’ Starfish, and galloping Seahorses. The production relies on adult volunteers to make the week and the performance a success. Adults who would like to volunteer can do so on the pre-registration form or during the auditions for the play. The Las Vegas Arts Council has been the local host organization for this program for more than 30 years.  This year, major financial support is being provided through a grant from the Las Vegas New Mexico Community Foundation.  Missoula Children’s Theatre is a traveling program. The tour directors bring all the costumes and props for the play. Your comment has been submitted.  Reported There was a problem reporting this. title: Mariachi Paisano del Valle to kick off Fiestas on Friday
body: Martin Sena, who once led mariachi programs at both Las Vegas school districts, plays alongside former students in a group called Mariachi Paisano del Valle. They will perform during the Fiestas de Las Vegas Mass at Our Lady of Sorrows Church on Friday, July 3, at 10 a.m. and then at Plaza Park until noon.  Martin Sena, who once led mariachi programs at both Las Vegas school districts, plays alongside former students in a group called Mariachi Paisano del Valle. They will perform during the Fiestas de Las Vegas Mass at Our Lady of Sorrows Church on Friday, July 3, at 10 a.m. and then at Plaza Park until noon. Martin Sena, who once led mariachi programs at both Las Vegas school districts, has reunited some of his former students to perform for the new Fiestas Reina and kick off Las Vegas’ biggest party. Mariachi Paisano del Valle, an Annual Fiesta Reunion, is scheduled to perform during the Fiestas de Las Vegas Mass at Our Lady of Sorrows Church on Friday, July 3, at 10 a.m. Sena, the mariachi band’s director, founder and trumpet player, said in an email statement to The Optic that after the Mass, the mariachi will walk from the church to Plaza Park alongside the Marisa Archuleta, the Fiestas Reina, and priests. Sena said the mariachi will then perform at Plaza Park until noon. The award-winning Mariachi Paisano del Valle was formed in 1997, as part of a mariachi program Sena helped start at Valley Middle School. The group has not missed playing at the Fiestas de las Vegas since, Sena said. The group has not missed the Fiestas Mass since 2000. Sena eventually went on to teach for Las Vegas City Schools, where he also led a mariachi program at Robertson High School. Sena’s former students continue to play with Mariachi Paisano del Valle. Sena said that, since the group’s members have moved on, they do not perform regularly together. “The fiestas are a special time that we reunite and get to perform together,” he said. “We all look forward to seeing each other and once again ... perform together as Mariachi Paisano del Valle.” Mariachi Paisano del Valle performs traditional mariachi music such as rancheras, boleros, huapangos, sones, and cumbias, Sena said. He said the group’s “number one hit by far” is “La Reina es el Rey,” as performed by lead vocalist and vihuela player Anita Montano Lopez. Audiences also often request songs they can dance to, Sena  said. “Of course people always ask for the cumbias, ‘El Mariachi Loco,’ ‘Camaron Pela’o,’ and ‘La Yaquesita,’ he said. As far as those in the mariachi band, they “love playing them all,” Sena said, but added that the songs played during the Fiestas Mass are especially favored by the group. Aside from Sena and Montano Lopez, Mariachi Paisano del Valle includes Christian Gutierrez on guitar; Joseph Wofel on guitarron; Andres Archuleta on trumpet, and Marcos Cano on accordion. The group’s name is in honor of one of Sena’s uncles, who moved away from the Las Vegas area but, when asking about what was happening at home, would say in Spanish, “Que se mira pa’l pais?” “‘El pais’ is where home was,” Sena said. “‘El pais’ is El Valle.” From this came the name, Mariachi Paisano del Valle, he said. Sena said he hopes the Fiestas audience will remember “the good old days” when the mariachi members were younger, but also see that they continue to represent the Las Vegas community “with the same amount of passion.” He noted the importance of mariachi music to the community. “Mariachi is part of our culture and tradition,” Sena said. “It defines who we are and is a form of folk art that should be preserved.” Your comment has been submitted. title: Man accused of threatening wife, children with gun
body: A Las Vegas man is facing multiple charges after allegedly punching his wife in the face and pointing a loaded gun at her and five children. Prosecutors charged 41-year-old Russell J. Taylor with five felony counts of child abuse and one felony count of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon following a June 25 altercation at his home north of Romeroville. New Mexico State Police responded just before 9 p.m. June 25 to a home on Roadrunner Road after a woman reported she’d been involved in a fight with her husband. The woman told police that Taylor had been drinking and that they got into a verbal argument, according to an affidavit filed in San Miguel Magistrate Court. She told police that during the argument, she said Taylor punched her in the face while he was holding their 2-year-old child, the affidavit stated. She told police that after striking her, Taylor went to his truck and grabbed a handgun, chambered a round and then pointed it at her while five children ranging in ages from 1 to 14 stood behind her. The 14-year-old child pleaded with him to put the gun down, and Taylor instructed the 14-year-old and a 7-year-old child to get into the truck, according to the affidavit. He then drove away with the two kids. Police searched the area but were unable to locate Taylor or the two children. At the time, Taylor was awaiting trial in a misdemeanor battery case. Under the conditions of release in the case, the court ordered that he cannot possess firearms or consume alcohol. The charges stemmed from a September 2025 incident where Taylor was charged with misdemeanor battery of a household member, court records show. He was released from jail on an unsecured bond ahead of a jury trial, which is scheduled to begin July 15. In May 2025, Taylor was charged with felony aggravated fleeing a law enforcement officer and misdemeanor charges of battery on a household member, interference with communications and criminal damage to the property of a household member. A jury trial in that case is scheduled to begin in October. Taylor was not in custody as of this writing but has retained an attorney in the latest case. In addition to the felony counts of child abuse and assault, he is also charged with one misdemeanor count of battery. Your comment has been submitted.  Reported There was a problem reporting this. title: New Mexico Disgraced ex-Dem majority leader finally headed to trial in huge corruption case
body: Nearly five years after federal agents raided the home of former New Mexico House Majority Leader Sheryl Williams Stapleton, the disgraced Albuquerque Democrat is finally set to face trial in one of the largest public corruption cases in recent New Mexico history. Williams Stapleton, once one of the most powerful Democrats in the New Mexico Legislature, appeared in court Thursday after federal prosecutors added two more tax fraud charges to her already sprawling federal case. She now faces 37 federal charges, including conspiracy to defraud the United States, money laundering, mail fraud, bribery involving programs receiving federal funds, fraud, and false statements. The federal trial is currently set for August 3. The case centers on allegations that Williams Stapleton used her positions at Albuquerque Public Schools and in the New Mexico Legislature to funnel millions of dollars connected to APS career and technical education programs through a Washington, D.C.-based company called Robotics Management Learning Systems. Investigators say Robotics was tied to Williams Stapleton’s co-defendant, Joseph Johnson. Prosecutors allege Williams Stapleton used Johnson’s company to divert federal grant money intended for educational programs and instead used the funds for personal and political benefit. According to the new report, federal prosecutors say Williams Stapleton embezzled $1,152,506 in federal grant funds — roughly 35% of the money APS paid to Robotics — and used the money for items including a home remodel, her family’s restaurant, her consulting company, trips, shopping, and vehicles. As she entered court Thursday, Williams Stapleton avoided eye contact with cameras. When KRQE asked, “What do you say to the people who believe you did something wrong?” her attorney, Ahmad Assed, responded, “We don’t have any comment at this time, thank you.” Inside the courtroom, the once-powerful lawmaker reportedly sat quietly and showed little emotion as she waited for the judge. Across the aisle was Johnson, her co-defendant. Both Williams Stapleton and Johnson pleaded not guilty to the additional charges. Prosecutors say both could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted. The long delay in the case has frustrated New Mexicans who watched the scandal explode in 2021, when Williams Stapleton resigned from the Legislature in disgrace after search warrants were served at her home and APS office. Before the federal indictment, Williams Stapleton had already been charged in state court in 2021. Her attorney said the existence of two separate cases helped slow the process. “This is a unique case in that Ms. Williams is facing two trials and the timeline with respect to trying the federal case first is paramount, before a state case is ensued,” Assed said. “And so that dynamic aided a lot in terms of delay with respect to trying the case.” But the allegations have never been simple. Piñon Post reporting from 2021 exposed how Williams Stapleton’s alleged scheme appeared to involve a web of political connections, nonprofits, shell companies, education funds, and longtime Democrat power players stretching back decades. Robotics Management Learning Systems was registered at a Washington, D.C., address connected to Johnson, who also operated National Corrections and Rehabilitation Corporation. Johnson was also listed as president of the Ujima Foundation, another entity tied to the alleged scheme. The relationship between Johnson and Williams Stapleton was not new. Piñon Post previously reported that Johnson and Williams Stapleton both had roots in New Mexico State University and New Mexico political circles dating back to the late 1970s and 1980s. Johnson later became a figure in former Democrat Gov. Toney Anaya’s administration, eventually rising to secretary of Health and Environment after a scandal involving state health contracts. Johnson was later charged in connection with bribery, fraud, conspiracy, kickbacks, and racketeering allegations from that era, though the charges were ultimately dismissed after a key witness recanted. He later returned to political work and became associated with Jesse Jackson’s Rainbow Coalition. Williams Stapleton also had ties to the Rainbow Coalition. Piñon Post previously noted that she was listed as the New Mexico contact for the group and was active in the organization in the late 1980s. Those old connections matter because prosecutors now allege the APS scheme relied on the same types of entities and political relationships that allowed millions in education funds to move with little scrutiny. At the Legislature, Williams Stapleton was not a backbencher. She was the second-highest-ranking Democrat in the New Mexico House and served for decades while also working as an APS administrator. Critics have long argued that dual role gave her unusual influence over education policy, appropriations, and public-school spending. Piñon Post previously reported that Williams Stapleton sponsored or supported legislation related to career and technical education — the same general area from which federal APS funds were allegedly diverted through Robotics. Prosecutors have alleged she used her legislative and APS positions to benefit herself financially. The scandal also renewed scrutiny over APS itself. Years before the federal indictment, KRQE investigative reporting found Williams Stapleton had been paid more than $100,000 by APS for work she allegedly did not perform while serving in the Legislature. Instead of being punished, APS leadership changed the rules to allow legislators employed by the district to continue being paid while serving in Santa Fe. Now, years later, the criminal case is finally nearing trial. For New Mexicans, the allegations are staggering: federal education money meant for students, a longtime Democrat lawmaker, a politically connected out-of-state company, alleged kickbacks, alleged money laundering, and more than $1.1 million prosecutors say was diverted for personal benefit. Williams Stapleton and Johnson are presumed innocent unless proven guilty. But the case has already become a symbol of how political power, weak oversight, and public money can create a corruption nightmare. The trial set for August could finally begin to answer the question New Mexicans have been asking since 2021: How did this alleged scheme go on for so long — and who else knew? title: Luisa G brings ‘brand new band’ to Fiestas on Friday
body: Luisa G is set to perform during the Fiestas de Las Vegas on Friday, July 3 from 3:35-4:45 p.m.  Luisa G is set to perform during the Fiestas de Las Vegas on Friday, July 3 from 3:35-4:45 p.m. Luisa G – known by her fans as ‘la Tejana Nuevomexicana’ –  is set to take the Plaza Park stage with her powerful voice and a brand new band on Friday, July 3 from 3:35-4:45 p.m. Along with her newly formed band, Grupo Nuevo Sonido, Luisa G will also open for the Blue Ventures on July 3 at Buffalo Hall. That show is set to take place from 8 p.m.-midnight. Advance tickets are $25. If purchased at the door, tickets are $30, Luisa G said. Tickets for the nighttime concert can be purchased from any member of the Blue Ventures, from Luisa G or at Buffalo Hall. Luisa G lives in Lubbock, Texas, but her father’s side of the family has roots in Guadalupita – a community located about 14 miles north of Mora. She described the music she performs – a mix of cover songs and her own compositions – as “New Mexico style to the bone,” with many of her songs being rancheras or “heartfelt valses.” Luisa G said that on Friday she will begin her performance with “Soy Nuevomexicana,” then follow it with “The Spanglish Cumbia.” Both songs are original compositions. “It’s really neat to have an original song and the people in the audience are singing along with you,” she said. “It’s a great feeling.” Luisa G has performed at the Fiestas at least four times; up until this year, she was accompanied by Sangre Joven. This will be the first time she will perform with Grupo Nuevo Sonido. “We’re a brand new band,” Luisa G said of Grupo Nuevo Sonido. “We’re calling this the ‘Por Primera Vez’ tour.” Local musician Daniel Lee Gallegos – the lead singer and guitarist for Sangre Joven – helped Luisa G realize her lifelong dream of becoming a singer and recording artist. Luisa G first “met” Gallegos in 2020, when he started posting videos of himself playing music on Facebook Live. Gallegos was making the videos as a way to “destress” following the worldwide shutdown caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Gallegos had lost his job at the Plaza Hotel and could no longer perform music for a live audience at that time. “The only way I could destress – and this really helped me out a lot – was to play music,” Gallegos said. “I picked up an acoustic guitar, turned on my phone, and put it on Facebook.” Luisa G said the pandemic years were also tough on her. The worldwide crisis forced her to face her own mortality. She said she wanted to leave a legacy behind for her family should anything happen to her. This thought, as well as Gallegos’ videos, inspired Luisa G to pursue singing. She bought one of Gallegos’ CDs and wrote him a note telling him that she had always wanted to record and asking if he knew of anyone who has a studio. Gallegos owns his own recording studio, SJ Records. “(Gallegos) reached out to me and the rest is history,” Luisa G said. “We’re now working on my seventh album.” Their correspondence led to Luisa G being a special guest on one of Gallegos’ videos. The video ended up being one of the top ones Gallegos posted to Facebook, garnering more than 60,000 views. “That was my first public performance,” Luisa G said. The friendship between Luisa G and Gallegos also led to Luisa G writing a song about him, called “Soy Músico de Corazón.” The song was awarded song of the year in 2025 by the New Mexico Hispanic Music Association. Luisa G and Sangre Joven no longer perform together due to scheduling conflicts, Luisa G said. Both she and Sangre Joven have become busy with their own endeavors, and she felt the need recently to create her own band. Members of Grupo Nuevo Sonido include Kiki Mondragon, a native of Denver, on keyboards; Dino Archuleta, who hails  from Alcalde, on bass guitar; Krystal Salazar, also from Alcalde, on drums; Ruben Dominguez from Abiquiu on guitar and Nico Quintana, of Albuquerque, also on guitar. Dominguez will not be able to make the Fiestas de Las Vegas, Luisa G said, but she and the rest of the band plan to be there. “I’m excited to be there,” Luisa G said. “And I’m excited to be there with my new band. And I’m excited to see all the people from Vegas and all the fans that come from everywhere.” Your comment has been submitted.  Reported There was a problem reporting this. title: Los Texmaniacs return to Vegas after 10-year hiatus
body: Los Texmaniacs are set to perform Saturday, July 4 from 8 p.m. to midnight at the Plaza Hotel ballroom. From left: Chris Rivera, the band’s drummer; Max Baca, vocalist and bajo sexto player; Josh Baca who plays the accordion and Noel Hernandez, vocalist and bass guitar player.  Los Texmaniacs are set to perform Saturday, July 4 from 8 p.m. to midnight at the Plaza Hotel ballroom. From left: Chris Rivera, the band’s drummer; Max Baca, vocalist and bajo sexto player; Josh Baca who plays the accordion and Noel Hernandez, vocalist and bass guitar player. Max Baca, lead singer and founding member of Los Texmaniacs, said he’s looking forward to breaking a decade-long hiatus this week when his band returns to Las Vegas. The last time Los Texmaniacs played during the Fiestas de Las Vegas was about 10 years ago, Baca said during a telephone interview with The Optic on June 25. The Grammy award-winning band is set to play the Fiestas again when they perform during a special dance on Saturday, July 4 from 8 p.m. to midnight at the Plaza Hotel ballroom. The dance will be free, Baca said. “I’m really excited about it, it means a lot,” Baca said of playing during the Fiestas. “I’m really proud to return to my home state and entertain the folks there in Las Vegas.” Los Texmaniacs – a band that Baca said plays “traditional roots music,” includes Baca on bajo sexto; Baca’s nephew, Josh Baca, on accordion; Noel Hernandez on bass and Chris Rivera on drums. All members of the band sing. Although he resides in San Antonio, Texas, Baca’s musical roots sprung in Northern New Mexico about five decades ago, he said. Baca’s musical career has included winning two Grammys and being a guest artist on a Rolling Stones album. Baca formed Los Texmaniacs in 1997, and since then the band’s regional Tejano sound, which includes a mix of blues, rock and jazz, has won two Grammys. The band is one of the first Chicano groups to tour China. Baca was born and raised in Albuquerque and got his start as a musician learning from his father – also named Max Baca – who played accordion with his own band, Max Baca y su Conjunto Norteño, for many years. Max Baca Sr. passed away 2002. Baca said his dad taught him how to play the accordion. “My dad was a master at polkas,” Baca said. Baca said he used to play the Fiestas de Las Vegas “all the time” with his father  and brother, Jimmy Baca. He recalled that they would often play with the husband-and-wife duet Ramon and Lydia. Baca also recalled having to learn to play the bass on the fly. One day, his father took him to a pawn shop and picked out a bass guitar for him. “He goes, ‘here, do you like this?’” Baca said his father asked him. He replied yes. “Cool,” the father said. “I’m going to buy it because I need a bass player for next weekend.” Baca said he had one week to learn to play the bass. Aside from the bass and accordion, he plays guitar and the bajo sexto – a Mexican string instrument with 12 strings. “It’s like the grizzly bear of guitars,” Baca said of the bajo sexto. “It has a beautiful sound.” In 1990, Max Baca joined the Texas Tornados – a Tejano music group known for revolutionizing Tex-Mex music. He played with them until 1999. While playing with the Texas Tornados, the band received a call from a representative of the Rolling Stones, asking whether Leonardo “Flaco” Jiménez – the band’s accordion player – would play on one of the band’s songs. Jiménez said yes, but also said that if the Stones wanted a true Tejano sound, they would need someone to play the bajo sexto on the track as well. Both Jiménez and Baca went on to play on “Sweethearts Together,” a song from the Stones’ 1994 album, “Voodoo Lounge.” “It was a dream come true,” Baca said of recording the song. He recalled that Rolling Stones guitarist Keith Richards took an interest in his bajo sexto. Richards asked to buy the instrument from Baca, who said the British rockstar told him to “name his price” three times. “I was starstruck. ... I was caught off guard,” Baca said of Richards’ proposition. Baca said that he felt the bajo sexto had a sentimental value and did not sell it. Baca moved to Austin, Texas, in 1997, the same year he formed Los Texmaniacs. The group won its first Grammy in 2010 for best Regional Mexican Tejano album. They won their second Grammy earlier this year for best regional roots album for their contribution to a tribute album to zydeco musician Clifton Chenier. In the nearly 30 years they’ve been in existence Los Texmaniacs have secured a steady following and have toured the world with their Tejano sound. “I never thought in my wildest dreams that I would win a Grammy, let alone record with the Rolling Stones,” Baca said of the experience. He has lived in San Antonio since 2002. He said he is “honored” to play the Fiestas once more. “I am honored to be back home, to my home state,” he said. Your comment has been submitted. title: Archuleta earns title of Fiesta Reina
body: Marisa Archuleta, 22, received the title of Reina during the Fiestas de Las Vegas Fiesta Queen Pageant at West Las Vegas High School cafeteria on Sunday.  Marisa Archuleta, 22, received the title of Reina during the Fiestas de Las Vegas Fiesta Queen Pageant at West Las Vegas High School cafeteria on Sunday. Two contenders for the title of  Reina shared their talents, personality and love of their community Sunday evening at the West Las Vegas High School cafeteria during the Fiestas de Las Vegas Fiesta Queen Pageant. In the end, 22-year-old Marisa Archuleta was given the title of 2026 Fiesta Reina and opponent Navaeh Gurule, 16, was given the title of Princesa. “It’s going to be an amazing experience,” Archuleta said just moments after receiving the Reina title. “I’m very thankful that I have this opportunity.” Archuleta looks forward to traveling the state and meeting those involved in Fiestas celebrations in other communities, as well as being a role model for others. She was thankful for all those who supported her, whether in person or online. She also expressed gratitude to Gurule. As the pageant began, Las Vegas Mayor David Romero took the stage and welcomed the crowd of about 150 people to the event. “For 138 years our Fiestas have celebrated the history, faith, culture and traditions that have shaped our community,” he said. The contestants were not only competing to wear a crown; they were offering to serve as ambassadors for Las Vegas. “The title of Reina represents leadership, character, community service and commitment to preserving the traditions that have been passed down to generations of Las Vegans,” Romero said. Romero thanked Gurule and Archuleta for choosing to represent Las Vegas, stating that regardless of who won that day they were helping to preserve a tradition. “Best of luck to each of our contestants and may tonight be a memorable celebration,” Romero said. “Que vivan las Fiestas.” Five judges scored Gurule and Archuleta for their performance in a series of rounds, including Fiesta attire, evening wear, a speech competition, a talent competition, an interview and an impromptu question. Ane Romero, who served as Fiestas Reina in 2001 and was Miss New Mexico in 2005, was the pageant’s emcee. She introduced the pageant’s judges: state treasurer and 1996 Fiestas Reina, Laura M. Montoya; Fred Sandoval, executive director of the National Latino Behavioral Health Association; Stephanie Cordova Levy, president and chairwoman of the Royal Court Committee of Taos; Olivia Romero, cofounder of the Ernestine Romero Scholarship Foundation; and Miguel Negrete, director of constituent services for Sen. Martin Heinrich. Ane Romero said she had received messages from the public complaining that they did not know any of the judges, with the exception of the state treasurer. “That’s the point,” Romero said. “It is our priority to ensure that we have judges from outside of the community to ensure fairness. … We know that in a small community, everyone knows who you are.” “We just wanted to ensure that our candidates had as fair a process as possible,” she said. Ane Romero acknowledged former Reinas who were in attendance. Jaiden Saiz, the 2025 Fiestas Reina, was invited to take the stage and discuss what the experience of being Reina and representing the community has meant for her. “It means so much, especially since my community is my hometown,” Saiz said. She said being Reina allowed her the opportunity to show how much she loves her community by representing it. Multi-award-winning vocalist Brenda Ortega provided musical entertainment. Mariachi Alma del Norte – a local group led by music teacher James Leger – also took the stage as part of Archuleta’s talent competition. Archuleta sings and plays guitar with Mariachi Alma del Norte. On Sunday, she sang “La Ley del Monte,” a song made popular by the late Mexican singer Vicente Fernández. Archuleta said her love of community and culture inspired her to run for Fiestas queen. “I enjoy being able to show my love for where I come from,” she said. The Fiestas Reina and Princesa will officially receive their crowns during a coronation Mass on Friday, July 3 at 10 a.m. at Our Lady of Sorrows Church. Your comment has been submitted. title: Romero ‘honored’ to serve as Fiestas grand marshal
body: Dr. Eric Romero has been named the 2026 Fiestas de Las Vegas grand marshal.  Dr. Eric Romero has been named the 2026 Fiestas de Las Vegas grand marshal. Dr. Eric Romero, a longtime educator who has taught – and fed – thousands by way of cultural events he helps organize, is set to lead the Fiestas de Las Vegas celebrations as grand marshal. Romero will ride in this year’s parade with his wife, retired bilingual educator Renee Romero, Saturday, July 4 starting at 9 a.m. “I’m honored,” Romero said of being chosen as this year’s grand marshal. He serves as director of Native American and Hispano Studies at New Mexico Highlands University. The institution also recently acknowledged his work with the community, naming him the Highlands Spirit Award Distinguished Honoree. “Dr. Eric Romero embodies the values of service, leadership, and cultural preservation honored by the Highlands Spirit Award,” states a social media post made by the university. “Dr. Romero believes education empowers people and strengthens communities, serving students as a mentor, advocate, and trusted guide.” Romero said he believes his work to uphold Northern New Mexico cultural traditions is the reason he was selected as this year’s grand marshal. Romero was instrumental in establishing NMHU’s matanza, which takes place every two years in October. Spanish for “slaughter” or “killing,” a matanza also refers to a community event in which an animal is butchered, cooked, and shared with family and friends. Romero noted that the matanza is a cultural tradition, not just a barbecue. “(The matanza) expresses cultural values of sustainability, sharing, gratitude, collaboration, mutualism,” Romero said. “Northern New Mexico communities have a history of collaborating and sharing resources, particularly in times of scarcity.” “We’ve always helped each other as a community,” he went on to say. “For me those values are more important than just eating together.” Romero was involved with matanza events that took place at the NMHU stadium about 20 years ago. There was a period of about 15 years when there were no matanzas on campus; however, they did continue for some time as private, off-campus events, Romero said. As faculty advisor for the student organization called MEChA – Movimiento Estudiantil Chicano de Aztlán – Romero helped coordinate the off-campus matanzas with students. Because they were held off campus, these events more closely resembled traditional matanzas in which a pig or goat is slaughtered at the site. These off-campus matanzas took place every year from 2010 until 2020, Romero said. It was former NMHU President Dr. Sam Minner who decided to bring back the matanza celebration to Highlands, Romero said. Romero was one of several people to design the NMHU Cultural Park – an area on the northeast corner of Melody Park designated for cultural events –  including the matanza. Completed in 2021, the Cultural Park includes an adobe bread oven and an underground pit. Matanza events have taken place there in 2021, 2023 and 2025, Romero said. Romero said the meat that is cooked at Highlands’ matanza events is given by donors. The animals are not slaughtered on site as would be done in a traditional matanza – health and safety regulations prohibit this from taking place on a college campus, he said. During the last matanza  in 2025, volunteers cooked about 800 pounds of beef and pork inside the Cultural Park’s underground pit, Romero said. An additional 600 pounds of chicharrones were cooked. Matanza events also involve chile roasting, corn roasting and the tying of ristras, Romero said. All who attend the matanza events eat for free. “It emphasizes (the) cultural value of sharing,” Romero said of matanzas. Romero’s work towards identifying and strengthening local cultural traditions has extended beyond the matanzas. At NMHU, he teaches a class called New Mexico Acequia Land Grant and Reservation Communities, in which he teaches about the cultural history of land stewardship and agricultural practices. Romero also seeks to strengthen traditional indigenous agricultural practices by participating in community-wide agricultural demonstrations. Romero teaches courses in sociolinguistics, in which he emphasizes the importance of the Northern New Mexico Spanish and seeks to find ways to revitalize it.  He said there are idiosyncrasies that are part of Northern New Mexico Spanish that are in danger of being lost. This is an area Romero shares in common with his wife, who was the founder of a dual language immersion program with the Las Vegas City Schools. Renee Romero also worked for West Las Vegas Schools as a Spanish teacher. “Between my wife and myself, I think we’ve had an impact in looking at traditional Northern New Mexico Spanish language revitalization,” Dr. Eric Romero said. The Romeros are originally from Colorado. Both attended the University of Arizona in Tucson, where Dr. Eric Romero completed a PhD in cultural linguistic anthropology and Renee Romero completed an undergraduate degree in bilingual education. She eventually attended NMHU, where she completed a master’s in curriculum and instruction. Before completing the doctoral program, Dr. Eric Romero was offered a position at NMHU teaching multicultural education. Although the Romeros had intended to move back to Colorado after completing their studies in Arizona, they decided to make their home in Las Vegas. They have been here since 1995. “Things fell into place for us to be here,” Romero said. “I’m pleased that it turned out that way.” Your comment has been submitted. title: New Mexico Leger Fernández loses it again over SAVE America Act
body: Democrat U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández is once again attacking Republican-backed election integrity reforms, claiming the push to require proof of citizenship and voter identification is part of an effort to make it harder for Americans to vote. In a series of social media videos, the far-left congresswoman from New Mexico’s Third Congressional District accused Republicans of shutting down Congress and holding the legislative process “hostage” over the SAVE America Act, a voter integrity proposal backed by President Donald Trump and House conservatives. “Republicans just shut down Congress to make it harder for you to vote,” Leger Fernández wrote on X. “That’s how scared they are of your power.” In the accompanying video, Leger Fernández stood outside in Washington, D.C., and claimed Republicans were not acting to “help the American people,” but instead trying “to take away your ability to register to vote.” “Unless you’re rich, have a passport, willing to pay more money to get documents, because you know what, that photo ID you have, that won’t count under their proposal,” she said. The claim fits a familiar Democrat talking point: requiring proof of citizenship or voter ID is somehow voter suppression, even though citizenship is already a basic requirement to vote in federal elections. The SAVE America Act would amend the National Voter Registration Act to require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections. The legislation lists multiple forms of acceptable proof, including a valid U.S. passport, certain REAL ID documents that indicate citizenship, military ID paired with a service record showing U.S. birthplace, a government-issued photo ID showing U.S. birthplace, or a government-issued photo ID paired with documents such as a birth certificate, naturalization certificate, certificate of citizenship, consular report of birth abroad, or certain other documents. That is far different from the simplified Democrat attack that voters would essentially need a passport to participate. Leger Fernández also attacked the bill over mail-in voting. “And they want to make sure we don’t have mail-in voting,” she said. “I tell you, mail-in voting makes it easier for rural people to vote, for military to vote, for people who might have kids at home and can’t take time out of their work to go vote.” She added, “So that’s what they’re trying to do, is to make it harder for you to vote.” The White House’s SAVE America Act page frames the proposal very differently, saying “American citizens — and only American citizens — should decide American elections.” It describes the proposal as requiring valid ID before registering to vote in a federal election, proof of citizenship, and restrictions on mail-in ballots except for illness, disability, military service, or travel. In another video posted one day earlier, Leger Fernández claimed Congress was being “held hostage by the most extreme members of the Republican Party.” Note: Over 80 percent of Americans support the provisions of the SAVE America Act. Despite that, she accused Republicans of demanding that a “voter suppression bill” be attached to “everything we pass.” “No, we are not going to suppress our elections,” she said. “We are not going to require that you have a passport to be able to vote.” She then added, “We’re going to say no to that.” Leger Fernández also said Congress should return to other business, including the National Defense Authorization Act, while making clear she opposes the proposed level of defense spending. “Listen, I’m against spending $1.4 trillion on defense, but we should be able to have a debate about that,” she said. Her comments came as a group of House Republicans pushed to force action on the SAVE America Act. The fight disrupted the House schedule and helped send lawmakers home early for the July 4 recess. But for most Americans, the issue is simple: requiring proof that a voter is a U.S. citizen should not be controversial. For Democrats like Leger Fernández, however, the proposal has become another opportunity to portray basic election safeguards as an attack on voters. Her argument effectively assumes many New Mexicans are unable to manage basic documentation requirements — an argument critics say is insulting to the very voters Democrats claim to defend. Leger Fernández has made similar claims before. In February, after the House passed the SAVE America Act, her office released a statement calling the bill “voter suppression, plain and simple.” She claimed it would make it “harder and more expensive” for citizens, “especially women, Native Americans, service members, and rural voters,” to register and vote. That framing turns a proof-of-citizenship requirement into an accusation that Republicans are targeting vulnerable groups. But the actual policy question is far narrower: should people registering to vote in federal elections be required to prove they are U.S. citizens? Republicans say yes. Leger Fernández says that is voter suppression. The clash comes as President Trump and the White House continue urging Congress to pass the SAVE America Act. Trump has described the issue as a national emergency and has used other legislative priorities to pressure Congress into acting. The result has been predictable: Republicans are pushing election integrity, while Democrats are warning of voter suppression, racism, hardship, and disenfranchisement. But to many New Mexicans, the Democrat meltdown may sound increasingly detached from common sense. Showing ID is required to board a plane, buy alcohol, enter many government buildings, cash a check, or pick up certain prescriptions. Yet when Republicans propose requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote, Leger Fernández insists the sky is falling. Her message is clear: asking voters to prove eligibility is too much. But why are Democrats so terrified of basic election security? Sangre Joven set to perform Friday
body: Left to Right: LaTrisha Padilla-Rythum Guitar; Daniel Lovato-Trumpet; Manuel Lucero-Drums; Daniel Lee Gallegos-Lead Guitar & Vocals; Amanda Audette-Trumpet; Richard “Combos” Maestas-Bass & Back Up Vocals; Ray Lucero-Saxophone Not Pictured  Left to Right: LaTrisha Padilla-Rythum Guitar; Daniel Lovato-Trumpet; Manuel Lucero-Drums; Daniel Lee Gallegos-Lead Guitar & Vocals; Amanda Audette-Trumpet; Richard “Combos” Maestas-Bass & Back Up Vocals; Ray Lucero-Saxophone Not Pictured Sangre Joven has been a band for nearly 40 years – but award-winning musician and Las Vegas native Daniel Lee Gallegos ensures that his band honors its name by playing the kind of music that keeps feet dancing and faces smiling. Sangre Joven is set to play at Plaza Park on Friday, July 3 from 1:30 p.m-3:45 p.m. The band is also scheduled to play that same day at El Rialto patio from 7-11 p.m. The evening performance is an event for all ages, Gallegos said. Advance tickets are $15; tickets will cost $25 at the door. Tickets are available at El Rialto and at the Music Album, Gallegos said. Sangre Joven has two new members for this year’s Fiestas: trumpet players Daniel Lovato from East Las Vegas and Amanda Audette from Los Alamos. The band also includes Gallegos as lead singer and lead guitar player; Manuel Lucero, from West Las Vegas, on drums; Richard Maestas, from Montezuma, on bass; LaTrisha Padilla, of Santa Fe, on rhythm guitar and Ray Lucero from Anton Chico on saxophone. The group, originally known as Sangre Nueva, started in 1987, Gallegos said. However, when they recorded their first cassette tape in 1989 they realized that a band in Texas already had that name. “We changed the name to Sangre Joven, which was fitting, my brother (Lorenzo) was 13 years old and I was 15 years old,” Gallegos said. Since 1987, Sangre Joven has been a staple here in Las Vegas, Gallegos said, noting that their 2023 album is called “El Orgullo de Las Vegas.” He said Sangre Joven has played the Fiestas every year since he can remember, bringing traditional musica ranchera that’s “very energetic, danceable and soothing to the heart.” Gallegos said audiences ask for songs they can dance to, such as rancheras, cumbias and valses. He described the band’s repertoire as Northern New Mexico music. The style of music is more upbeat and energetic than TexMex or music from the southern region of the state, he said. Gallegos said Sangre Joven has received several awards from the New Mexico Hispano Music Association, including Original Song of the Year, Bilingual Song of the Year, Instrumental Song of the Year and Traditional Ranchera of the Year. Gallegos owns his own recording studio, SJ Records, where he records himself and other musical acts. As a producer, he has won Producer of the Year four times and recorded 24 studio albums, he said. Fifteen of those albums are Sangre Joven albums, six feature Gallegos as a solo artist and three albums feature Gallegos playing music with his younger brothers in a band called Los Gallegos Brozz. About 80 percent of the music Gallegos has put out in a band or as a solo artist are cover songs, he said. The rest is original music. Gallegos has been able to be a full-time musician since the COVID-19 pandemic. Due to the pandemic, he lost his job at the Plaza Hotel, where he had worked for 16 years. Opportunities to perform live dried up as the world shut down. “I got depressed,” he said. “I got stressed out.” Music, which had always been a positive outlet, continued to be so during that time, Gallegos said. He said he picked up an acoustic guitar and filmed himself performing songs on Facebook Live. The simplified performances, he said, were meant to resemble times in the 1970s and ’80s when he would get together with loved ones and play music. “Our form of entertainment for our family … was playing music with acoustic guitars,” Gallegos said. He performed on Facebook every Friday for a year. The first Facebook Live shows that Gallegos did got about 2,000 viewers. By the end of the 60th show he had 89,000 viewers. Gallegos said he played the Facebook Live shows by himself at first, but then started to invite guests to do the show with him. “I was really just helping out myself, to destress myself,” he said. “But little did I know that I was helping out thousands and thousands of people because everybody was stuck at home.” The Friday Night shows, as Gallegos called them, helped his musical career “big time.” “It catapulted my career to a different level,” he said. He said that, to this day, he meets people who thank him for keeping them entertained during the pandemic. Gallegos said he also hopes to entertain during the Fiestas de Las Vegas. “If I see somebody smiling and having a good time and dancing I’ve done my job,” Gallegos said. “There’s a saying that goes, ‘con la música se alegra el corazón,’ which means with music the heart gets happy.” “That’s what I want, for people to be happy,” Gallegos said. title: City of Las Vegas Announces Zero-Tolerance Fireworks Enforcement
body: Public safety remains the City of Las Vegas' highest priority as residents and visitors prepare to celebrate the Fourth of July. With severe drought conditions and an elevated risk of wildfire, the City is taking a firm stance on illegal fireworks. Residents and visitors are expected to comply with all local fireworks laws, and violations will be met with strict enforcement. According to the NOAA National Integrated Drought Information System, San Miguel County, including the City of Las Vegas, is currently experiencing D2 – Severe Drought conditions. The City of Las Vegas is also under Stage 2 Water Restrictions, requiring increased water conservation due to limited water supplies. With extremely dry grasses and vegetation throughout the area, a single illegal firework can quickly start a wildfire. These conditions leave no room for complacency. Residents are expected to comply with all City fireworks regulations. Illegal fireworks put lives, property, and first responders at risk and will be enforced accordingly. The City of Las Vegas Fireworks Ordinance (City Code Chapter 238) is one of the most restrictive in New Mexico (See attached graphic). Pursuant to the New Mexico Fireworks Licensing and Safety Act (NMSA 1978, Sections 60-2C-1 through 60-2C-11), municipalities are authorized under Section 60-2C-7(C) to prohibit aerial fireworks and ground audible devices by local ordinance. The following fireworks are prohibited within the City of Las Vegas: Aerial fireworks, including bottle rockets, Roman candles, missiles, helicopters, reloadable mortars, aerial shells, mines, and any device designed to launch into the air. Ground audible devices, including firecrackers, chasers, and any fireworks that produce loud explosive reports. The sale of these prohibited fireworks is also illegal within city limits. In addition, open burning is prohibited year-round under City Code Chapter 154 to help reduce the risk of preventable fires. Residents should be aware that fireworks prohibited within the City of Las Vegas may still be legally sold in the unincorporated areas of San Miguel County and elsewhere in New Mexico where local ordinances permit their sale. However, purchasing these fireworks outside city limits does not make them legal to possess or use within the City of Las Vegas. The City will maintain zero-tolerance enforcement throughout the Independence Day holiday. The Las Vegas Police Department, Las Vegas Fire Department, and Code Enforcement Division will actively patrol and enforce City Code Chapter 238. Individuals found using or possessing prohibited fireworks within city limits will be cited, and illegal fireworks will be confiscated. Violators may face fines of up to $500, imprisonment for up to 90 days, or both, as authorized by City Code Chapter 238. Anyone responsible for starting a fire may also be held financially responsible for fire suppression costs, property damage, restitution, and any additional civil or criminal penalties authorized under New Mexico law. The City needs the public's help in identifying and reporting illegal fireworks. Because fireworks are often discharged in multiple locations across the community, it can be difficult for officers to pinpoint the exact source of the activity. Prompt and accurate reports from residents help law enforcement respond more quickly and effectively. Anyone who witnesses the use of illegal fireworks within the City of Las Vegas is encouraged to contact the Las Vegas Police Department Non-Emergency Dispatch at (505) 425-7504, Option 1. Call 9-1-1 only to report an active fire or another life-threatening emergency. Rather than risking a citation or causing a wildfire, the City encourages everyone to attend the professional Fourth of July fireworks display on Saturday, July 4, at dusk at the NMHU Golf Course. The show will be conducted by a licensed professional fireworks company in a carefully planned and controlled environment with firefighters, law enforcement officers, emergency medical personnel, and other public safety personnel on site. "Our community's safety comes first," said Fire Chief Steven Spann. "There will be no warnings for illegal fireworks this holiday. If you choose to violate the ordinance, you should expect to be cited. We encourage everyone to celebrate safely by attending the City's professional fireworks display and helping us protect our community." "We all enjoy celebrating the Fourth of July, but no celebration is worth putting lives or homes at risk," said Police Chief Caleb Marquez. "Help us protect our community by following the law, making smart decisions, and leaving the fireworks to the professionals whenever possible." While the City discourages the use of fireworks due to current drought and fire conditions, residents choosing to use allowable fireworks should do so responsibly. Use fireworks only on a non-combustible surface away from dry grass, brush, vehicles, and structures. Keep a bucket of water nearby and use it wisely, as the City is currently under Stage 2 Water Restrictions. Under the New Mexico Fireworks Licensing and Safety Act (NMSA 1978, Chapter 60, Article 2C), only individuals 16 years of age or older may use fireworks. Never use fireworks while intoxicated, discharge fireworks from or at a motor vehicle, or relight a malfunctioning firework. Completely soak used fireworks in water before disposing of them. If a fire starts, call 911 immediately. The City of Las Vegas thanks residents and visitors for their cooperation in helping prevent fires and ensuring a safe Independence Day for everyone.
